name: CBT-I
lead: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, multi-component treatment for chronic insomnia that combines techniques such as stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, relaxation and sleep hygiene.[1] It is described as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.[1][2]

The American College of Physicians (2016) recommends CBT-I as initial treatment for chronic insomnia in adults, and a 2015 meta-analysis reported benefits on diary measures of sleep.[2][3] Digital versions have been tested in randomized trials.[4]
In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned as the evidence-based option for people whose poor sleep affects appearance; no studies were found linking it to appearance outcomes.
infobox: Stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, relaxation, sleep hygiene[1]

paras: Stimulus control aims to link the bed with sleep, for example by getting up after about twenty minutes awake. Sleep restriction temporarily limits time in bed based on sleep efficiency and adjusts it gradually. Cognitive therapy and relaxation training are also used.[1]
CBT-I can be delivered by therapists or through internet or app-based programs. Meta-analyses of internet-delivered and digital CBT-I reported efficacy in randomized trials.[4][5]

Sleep restriction can cause fatigue, sleepiness, headaches, irritability and appetite changes that usually ease; it is not recommended where sleepiness is unsafe, and may worsen epilepsy. Relaxation training can cause paradoxical anxiety in some patients, stimulus control can be hazardous for people at high risk of falls, and CBT-I in bipolar disorder may raise the risk of switching to mania.[1]

A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis in Annals of Internal Medicine examined CBT-I's efficacy on diary measures of sleep in adults with chronic insomnia.[3] The American College of Physicians guideline of 2016 drew on randomized trials to recommend CBT-I as initial treatment.[2] A JAMA Internal Medicine meta-analysis examined CBT-I for insomnia comorbid with psychiatric and medical conditions.[6] Meta-analyses of internet-delivered and digital CBT-I have also been published.[4][5] No studies found on CBT-I for appearance outcomes.

claims.believers: Proponents cite guidelines and say it avoids medication.
claims.experts: The ACP guideline and meta-analyses support CBT-I as first-line treatment.[2][3]

claims.believers: Users say better sleep improves skin and eyes.
claims.experts: No studies found linking CBT-I to appearance outcomes.

card.summary: The guideline-recommended first-line therapy for chronic insomnia; nothing tested on looks directly.
card.note: Sleep restriction can cause daytime sleepiness; not suitable for everyone.

quick.overview:
CBT-I is a structured program that changes sleep-related habits and thoughts to treat chronic insomnia. Guidelines such as the American College of Physicians' recommend it first.

Looksmaxxing communities mention it for sleep quality; no studies were found testing effects on appearance.
quick.mechanism: It combines stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy and relaxation to rebuild the association between bed and sleep.
quick.risks: Sleep restriction can temporarily cause fatigue and sleepiness, and some conditions such as epilepsy or bipolar disorder call for caution.
